criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (and matches Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper examines river-basin water resource governance, deliberative watershed committees, and bulk water charges (cobranca) for raw water withdrawals/pollution in Brazil, explicitly noting in Footnote 1 (p. 602) that bulk water does not refer to water brought to households by water companies.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance factors in the water sector (São Paulo Law 7663/91, the 1997 National Water Law, creation of the National Water Agency ANA, deliberative river-basin committees, bulk water permits, and bulk water charges/cobranca). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow rule-type reading because the legal and regulatory mechanisms examined govern regional river-basin water resources and raw bulk water withdrawals/effluent dilution by utilities, industries, energy generators, and irrigators rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. (Overall decision is exclude under both readings due to failing Criteria 1 and 4.)
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3: qualitative empirical political-institutional case study drawing on primary interviews in São Paulo and Brasília and research from the multidisciplinary Watermark Project (Projeto Marca d'Água) across 20 Brazilian river basins.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: reports political, legislative, and institutional outcomes (enactment of state and federal water laws, creation of river-basin committees and ANA, and initiation of bulk water billing in the Paraíba do Sul basin), with no outcome measuring household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Qualitative political-institutional case study design is identifiable, with river basins and state/federal policy arenas in Brazil as units of analysis, but fails Criterion 5 with respect to review scope because no household or community service-access population or service-access outcome is examined.

evidence_quotes.quote: Bulk water thus does not refer to the water brought to households or industries by water companies, but only the water in rivers, streams, lakes or subterranean water tables.

The reforms also introduce a new water management tool, bulk water charges, through which industries, farmers, water and sanitation companies and other ‘bulk water users’ would have to pay for the water that they withdraw directly from rivers or lakes or that they pollute.

Focusing on the politics of reform legislation in the state of São Paulo and nationally, the article examines how political-institutional features of federalism and executive-legislative relations constrained the passage of reform legislation, and how pro-reform actors attempted to surmount such institutional limitations with networking strategies and by fostering incremental changes in practices on the ground.

The information contained in this article was collected through interviews by Keck in São Paulo and Abers in Brasília, as well as through research by participants in the Watermark Project (Projeto Marca d’Água), a multidisciplinary study of the development of decentralized water management institutions in 20 Brazilian river basins over 5–10 years.

Instead of a decentralized system of watershed committees and agencies to make decisions and implement cobrança, Ceará simply created a state level agency, COGERH, which, among other attributions, is responsible for implementing water charges for the whole state.

raw_response.exposure: Federalism, executive-legislative relations, bureaucratic competition, and policy networks shaping state (São Paulo) and federal water resource management legislation, river-basin committees, and bulk water charges (cobranca)
raw_response.outcome: Passage and institutional implementation of decentralized river-basin governance legislation, creation of watershed committees and the National Water Agency (ANA), and operationalization of bulk water charging in Ceará and the Paraíba do Sul basin
raw_response.population_and_sample: State and federal water resource policy arenas and river basins in Brazil (focusing on São Paulo state, the 1997 National Water Law, ANA, Ceará, and the Paraíba do Sul river basin; informed by interviews and the 20-basin Watermark Project)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E01: Wrong topic, corresponding to Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although empirical (qualitative case study using interviews and the 20-basin Watermark Project), the article examines the political and legislative construction of integrated river-basin water resource governance, stakeholder watershed committees, and raw bulk water charges (cobranca) in Brazil. It explicitly notes that bulk water refers to raw water in rivers, lakes, and aquifers rather than water delivered to households by utilities, and it reports no household or community water or sanitation service-access outcomes. Under both the plain wording of Criterion 2 (where c2=yes) and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (where c2=no), the paper is excluded because Criteria 1 and 4 are not met.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative political-institutional comparative case study (interviews and multi-basin field research)
